title: The sky didn’t turn dark because of clouds.
paragraphs: The sky didn’t turn dark because of clouds.
It turned dark because of wings.
And in a single terrifying day, an empire learned a lesson it had refused to hear.
This was the Eighth Plague God sent upon Egypt.
For generations, the people of Egypt had enslaved the Israelites. Families were broken. Children were oppressed. Hope was buried under chains.
Then God raised a deliverer: Moses.
Through him, God gave Pharaoh a simple command:
But Pharaoh’s heart hardened like stone.

Water turned to blood.
Frogs flooded homes.
Gnats covered skin.
Flies invaded the land.
Livestock died.
Boils covered bodies.
Hail shattered crops.
Then came the warning that would devastate what little remained.

“If you refuse to let my people go, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country.”
— Exodus 10:4

“The LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day and all that night… and the east wind brought the locusts.”
— Exodus 10:13
Imagine standing in Egypt that morning.
At first, it looked like dust on the horizon.
Because the swarm was so massive that the land itself grew dark.

“They covered the face of the whole land, so that the land was darkened.”
— Exodus 10:15
Whatever survived the hailstorm of the seventh plague was now devoured.

Leaves stripped.
Fruit erased.
Grain consumed.
A kingdom that once overflowed with abundance suddenly stared at famine.
Locusts crawled across rooftops, fields, and roads.
The sound alone must have been terrifying — millions of wings beating like a living storm.
He called Moses and Aaron and confessed:

“I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you.”
— Exodus 10:16
For a moment, it seemed like repentance had come.
And God sent a strong west wind that carried the locusts away and threw them into the Red Sea.
But Pharaoh’s heart hardened once more.
The most terrifying plague in the story was not the locusts.
He saw God’s power with his own eyes.
And still he refused to bow.
That disease still lives in the human heart today.
And slowly, the heart grows resistant to God’s voice.
But the story of Exodus does not end in destruction.
Because the plagues were not only judgments.
God was revealing that the idols of Egypt had no power — not the sun, not the river, not the gods of harvest.
The Exodus story points forward to a greater rescue.
Centuries after Moses confronted Pharaoh, another Deliverer stepped into history.
Where Pharaoh hardened his heart, Jesus humbled Himself.
Where sin demanded judgment, Jesus took the punishment upon the cross.

“God demonstrates His own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
— Romans 5:8
The real plague of humanity is not insects.
But the cure is the grace of Christ.
Through Jesus, hearts of stone can become hearts of flesh.
So the question from Exodus still echoes across time.
Or will you surrender to the One who gave His life to save you?
Because the greatest miracle is not a swarm of locusts leaving Egypt.
The greatest miracle is a stubborn heart finally surrendering to God.

Because the same God who shook Egypt
still changes hearts today.
